notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses from the Tent of Meeting right after the tabernacle was completed and filled with God's glory. Because God now dwelt in the midst of Israel, He gave Moses instructions on how the people could draw near to Him in worship. This showed that God wants close fellowship with His people.

God told Moses that any Israelite could bring an offering from their domesticated cattle, sheep, or goats. Wild animals could not be offered because sacrifices had to come from an owner's personal property and daily livelihood. An offering to God was meaningful because it cost the worshipper something real.

A burnt offering from the herd had to be a male animal without any disease or defect. The worshipper brought it freely to the entrance of the courtyard so that God would accept it. Giving the healthiest and most valuable animal reflected wholehearted surrender to the Lord.

The worshipper placed a hand firmly on the animal's head to show that the victim stood in their place. This ceremony brought atonement, which means removing sin and restoring a right relationship between a guilty person and God. It taught that God graciously accepts a substitute on behalf of the sinner.

differ.view: The sacrifice made atonement sacramentally, directing the worshipper's faith forward to the true propitiatory sacrifice of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars emphasize that the Hebrew word for atonement fundamentally means wiping clean, purging, or appeasing, rather than merely covering over sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching views the whole burnt offering as an act recognizing God's absolute lordship over creation, which brought atonement when offered with a sincere heart.

notes.meaning: The worshipper killed the young bull before the Lord, acknowledging that sin deserves death. Then Aaron's sons, the priests, caught the blood and splashed it against all sides of the altar. The shed blood represented life given up to make peace with God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient translations like the Septuagint indicate that the priests, rather than the lay worshipper, slaughtered the animal.

notes.meaning: The animal was skinned and then cut into its natural limbs and joints. The skin was the only part not burned on the altar fire, and it was later given to the officiating priest. Preparing the pieces carefully showed reverence for a holy gift.

The priests arranged the firewood on the altar to keep the flame burning steadily. Although the altar fire was first kindled by God from heaven, the priests were assigned to feed it with wood every day. Serving God required faithful, ongoing care by His appointed ministers.

Aaron's sons arranged the severed pieces, along with the head and the choice suet fat, on top of the burning wood. The fat helped the fire burn brightly so the entire offering was consumed. Laying the parts out in an orderly way honored God's house.

The internal organs and legs were washed with clean water to remove any dirt or impurities. The priest then burned the entire animal on the altar as a pleasing aroma, signifying that God warmly accepted the worshipper's whole devotion. It pointed to the clean heart and pure walk God desires in His people.

differ.view: The altar fire did not represent God's judicial wrath consuming the sacrifice, but His gracious acceptance of a dedicated life after forgiveness had already occurred.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars explain that the Hebrew term often translated 'offering made by fire' originally had the general sense of a food gift presented to God.

notes.meaning: If a worshipper could not afford a bull, God allowed them to bring a male sheep or goat without defect. God made worship accessible to ordinary families while still requiring their very best. The sacrifice had to be completely unblemished, just like the larger herd animals.

The sheep or goat was slaughtered on the north side of the altar before the Lord. Aaron's sons then caught its blood and splashed it against all sides of the altar. This followed the exact same pattern of substitution and blood atonement as the offering of a bull.

The worshipper cut the animal into pieces, and the priest arranged the pieces, the head, and the fat upon the wood on the altar. Every part was handled with the same dignity and order given to larger offerings. No gift was treated as second-rate before God.

The legs and internal organs were washed with water to make sure the offering was clean and pure. The priest then burned the entire animal on the altar fire as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. God accepted the sheep or goat just as readily as the costlier bull.

For those too poor to afford a sheep or goat, God provided the option of bringing turtledoves or young pigeons. These birds were plentiful, inexpensive, and easy to obtain in the land. God opened the way so that poverty would never keep someone from worshipping Him.

Because a bird was so small, the priest handled the slaughtering at the altar itself rather than having the worshipper do it. He pinched or wrung off the bird's head, burned it on the altar, and drained its blood against the side. This ensured that even the smallest offering was presented properly.

The priest removed the bird's digestive crop with its waste and tossed it into the ash pile on the east side of the altar. The east side was farthest from the Most Holy Place, showing that unclean things must be cast out of God's presence. Only what was clean could be burned on the altar.

The priest tore the bird open by its wings without tearing it into two separate halves, and burned it on the altar. Even though this was the gift of a poor person, it rose up as a pleasing aroma to the Lord just like a bull. God looks at the sincerity and devotion of the heart, not the market value of the gift.
